item.title: An Alaska storm scattered artifacts. Archaeologists are racing to save what's left
item.description: Last year, remnants of a typhoon damaged homes, infrastructure and an archaeological dig site. Now, archaeologists are trying to get as many objects out as possible before the next storm.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: Editor Rose Friedman, who helped shape NPR's cultural coverage, dies at 38
item.description: Friedman was in her early 20s when she landed her first position as an editorial assistant at NPR. She became an editor and reporter, and a co-creator of the annual Books We Love reading guide.

item.title: 'Joyful protestors' talk about the cultural value of the Kennedy Center
item.description: The center, a beacon of American arts and culture, is slated to be closed after a board vote. On Friday, a group called Hands Off the Arts is holding what they call a "joyful protest" outside.

item.title: There's 'Hope' for this divisive alien invasion film that mixes art and schlock
item.description: Shape-shifting aliens attack a South Korean border town in Hope, a big-budget thriller that blends third-rate CGI with exhilarating action scenes.

item.title: Remembering jazz singer Cassandra Wilson
item.description: Wilson, who died Sept. 1, spiced her singing with funk, hip-hop and blues. Kevin Whitehead offers an appreciation, and we listen back to Terry's 1988 interview with Wilson.

item.title: 'Looney Tunes' animator Chuck Jones explains what makes Wile E. Coyote tick
item.description: Jones, who died in 2002, shared the specific rules he had for the characters he co-created in this 1989 interview: "The roadrunner can never harm the coyote; the coyote could only harm himself."

item.title: Ms. Rachel has entered her album era, and she is so happy about it
item.description: Ms. Rachel has conquered YouTube, Netflix and the toy aisle. Now she's making an album, with real instruments, big feelings and her littlest listeners in mind.

item.title: Judge rules court must get notice as Trump threatens to tear down Kennedy Center
item.description: A judge told President Trump Thursday that he can't tear down The Kennedy Center –- at least not without 30 days' notice.

item.title: Attorney fighting Trump's efforts to rename and close Kennedy Center discusses case
item.description: NPR's Michel Martin speaks with Norm Eisen, whose legal group Democracy Defenders Action has been fighting the Trump administration in court over its efforts to rename and close the Kennedy Center.

item.title: Trump threatens to tear down the Kennedy Center, as legal battle continues
item.description: The president made the remark to reporters amidst back-and-forth developments in federal court, including an allegation that a forklift repeatedly struck the center.
